deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It holds a single methodological aphorism of six lines in ink, ending in a long horizontal stroke. Translation: 'A scientific advance is often merely the overcoming of a prejudice. Until then one has simply walked past the most obvious and most fruitful truths, because the prejudice directed attention toward the habitual ways of posing questions.'

There is nothing to reconstruct mathematically.

Context: the previous page records Hilbert's reflections on Cantor's letters. Topics there are the problem of 'finished' (fertig, i.e. completed) totalities, such as the system of all transfinite numbers versus the system of all sets; the continuum hypothesis as 'very hard'; and a proposal to treat 'irrational number' as a label for a fixed fact rather than as an existing thing. The next page (numbered 93) holds further aphorisms on the value of mathematics, Gauss, figures as 'drawn formulas', and his Festschrift (Grundlagen der Geometrie, 1899).

The aphorism fits this setting, circa 1897-1900. It reads naturally as a comment on how set-theoretic and foundational progress (Cantor, the axiomatic method) comes from discarding entrenched assumptions about legitimate questions. It anticipates the methodological optimism of the 1900 Paris problems address, which stresses that failures in solving problems often come from not having found the right standpoint or way of posing the question.

results.what: Methodological aphorism: scientific progress often consists merely in overcoming a prejudice that had steered attention to habitual questions, so that obvious and fruitful truths were overlooked.
results.modern_name: Philosophy of science remark (cf. later ideas of paradigm-bound inquiry, Kuhn 1962), not a mathematical result
results.usually_credited_to: General commonplace; related themes in Mach, and later Kuhn

deep.surprise_reason: This is a non-technical aphorism, fully in keeping with Hilbert's known methodological views (Paris address 1900, Grundlagen der Geometrie period). It is interesting as a biographical and intellectual-history detail, especially next to the Cantor and set-theory notes, but it contains no mathematical content and nothing unexpected.
transcription_corrections: Line 3: the manuscript reads 'bisdahin' written as one word (= 'bis dahin'); the transcription's separation is fine as normalization.
'blos' is legible as 'blos' (old spelling of 'bloß'), so the '[?]' can be removed.
There is a faint pencil page/folio number at the upper left, apparently '91' (or bleed-through). It is not in the transcription and is consistent with the next page being numbered 93.
The final word 'richtete' is followed by a period and a long horizontal closing stroke, not a separate textual element.
